t: Samaritans hold that there is one God, YHWH, that the Torah given to Moses is the only true holy book, and that Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem, is the place God chose.

Scholars see Samaritanism as taking shape as a distinct tradition in the Hasmonean and Roman era, after John Hyrcanus destroyed the Gerizim temple around 120 BCE; Samaritan tradition traces the separation to a schism in the time of the High Priest Eli.
About 900 registered communal Samaritans remain in 2025; they take this small number to be the fulfilment of a scriptural prophecy and hope for the Taheb, the Restorer.
dyk: Samaritans hold that the Binding of Isaac took place on Mount Gerizim, not at Jerusalem's Temple Mount, and in their version of the Ten Commandments the tenth commands an altar to be built on Gerizim.
ev: The Hasmonean ruler and high priest John Hyrcanus destroys the temple on Mount Gerizim and brings Samaria under his control
The date given for the Memar Markah, theological treatises attributed to Hakkam Markha
The Samaritan revolts of the 5th and 6th centuries are followed by Byzantine persecution that practically annihilates the Samaritans
Abu Al Hassan writes the Kitab at-Tabbah, a halakhic text
Abu'l-Fath writes a major work of Samaritan history, the Kitab al-Tarikh
From this year the oldest member of the priestly family is chosen as High Priest

f.origin: Samaria, around Mount Gerizim. Samaritans trace their separate history to a schism in the time of the High Priest Eli; scholars see a distinct tradition emerging in the Hasmonean and Roman era, with the temple on Gerizim built in the 5th century BCE.
f.founder: none: Samaritanism holds itself to be the faith the Israelites kept under Moses, whom it regards as the final prophet; after him the only authority is the successive Samaritan priesthood, from the line of Aaron.
f.scriptures: The Samaritan Pentateuch (the Torah), the only scripture; Samaritans also keep a variation of the Book of Joshua, which they do not regard as scripture, and chronicles, halakhic texts, midrash and liturgy.
